newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Uganda discuss Zaire's uncertain future.
newsitem.headline: France, Uganda discuss Zaire's uncertain future.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and visiting Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni expressed concern at the deepening conflict in Zaire when they met in Paris on Tuesday, French officials said.
"The situation is extremely serious and both presidents are worried," Chirac's spokeswoman, Catherine Colonna, said after the two leaders met for 75 minutes.
"They also expressed their attachment to the principle of the inviolability of borders which is a basic principle for international life and particularly for Africa," she said.
Museveni made no comment as Chirac accompanied him to the steps of his Elysee palace office, but the Ugandan leader was due to hold a news conference later.
France, a major power in Africa, has been at odds with Uganda for several years over conflicts in the Great Lakes region of central Africa.
Paris suspects Kamapla, with U.S. acquiesence, of aiding and abetting Rwandan-backed rebels who have captured a swathe of Zairean territory along the borders with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.

The U.N. Security Council called on Friday for the withdrawal of all foreign forces from Zaire, Africa's third largest state. The United States said last week it had urged all three neighbouring countries to stay out of the fighting.
The Kinshasa has repeatedly accused the three of direct involvement in the war which they deny.

France, which has long supported veteran Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, is urgently seeking an international conference on the Great Lakes region to halt hostilities and prevent the breakup of Zaire in chaos.
Officials said Chirac would try to enlist Museveni's agreement to a conference and his cooperation in holding back the advance of the Zaire rebels.

"We have no doubt that President Museveni can contribute to a cessation of hostilities in the region and to the emergence of solutions," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters.

French officials say the rebels, led by ethnic Tutsis, coordinate their activities with Rwanda's Tutsi authorities who in turn, are closely allied with Uganda which helped them seize power from a French-backed, Hutu-led government in 1994.
But Paris believes the key to halting the conflict may lie with Washington which is closely tied to Uganda and Rwanda.
French analysts say the government believes the United States is trying to edge it out of the last region where France still wields influence left over from its colonial past.

After months of transatlantic squabbling over Africa, French officials say the Americans appear to have come round to their view that a collapse of Zaire could de-stabilise the whole of central Africa and would not be in U.S. interests.

The United States backs the proposed conference. But sceptics say Washington may be paying lip service to the idea to placate Paris while hoping the rebellion will have spread to Kinshasa before the conference gets off the ground.
Burundi Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama was in Paris last week and indicated clearly he did not want outside powers to take a decisive hand in a settlement.

A European Union envoy has suggested a regional meeting be held prior to any international conference, a solution that might be more to Museveni's liking. French Humanitarian Action Minister Xavier Emmanuelli suggested a pre-conference should be held on the urgent refugee problem.
There are few reliable statistics, but French officials say they take seriously reports that up to 100,000 people have died of hunger, disease and war since the fighting began last year.

An estimated 400,000 refugees -- half of them in camps and half on the move -- are in the region between the rebel-held zone and the ragged Zairean army's front headquarters, the French officials say.
